A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IQ-MPC research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated and newly added content to be matched reliably.

before.justification: V1 reports original DMControl, MyoSuite and ManiSkill2 experiments, including learning curves, success rates, visual control, reward recovery and ablations.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, regularization sensitivity, noisy-dynamics evaluation, reward correlations and training-time measurements.

M1.justification: The encoder, latent dynamics, critic, policy prior, learning losses, gradient penalty and MPPI planner remain unchanged. Algorithm 2 drops an unused reward field from the buffer-insertion tuple, without changing the learning equations. Policy-prior-only interaction appears as a timing-study variant.

E1.justification: The benchmark tasks and visual-input coverage are retained. Appendix E.5 adds stochastic-transition Walker Run scenarios with trembling probabilities 0.01 and 0.02. The other new analyses reuse environments already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: HyPE joins the main locomotion and MyoSuite comparisons in Figures 2–3 and Table 1. HyPER is added specifically to the computational-cost comparison in Figure 16. Table 7 also introduces IQL+SAC as a reward-recovery comparator, whereas v1's recovery analysis showed IQ-MPC alone.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include an alpha sweep over 0.25, 0.5 and 1, controlled transition noise, Pearson correlation as a reward-recovery metric, and training-time comparisons with MPC versus policy-prior interaction. Existing architecture and default settings remain. Shorter Figure 2 time ranges establish changed reporting windows, but do not establish reruns or reduced actual training budgets.

E4.justification: V2 adds regularization sensitivity on Humanoid Walk, robustness to noisy Walker Run transitions, quantitative reward-recovery analysis across four tasks, and computational analysis including the cost of planning. These address questions absent from v1. The original demonstration-count, objective-formulation and gradient-penalty ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Three-seed averaging, success-rate tables with plus/minus values, and shaded variability already appear in v1 and remain in v2. No increased run count or new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedure is stated. The added Pearson coefficients serve as evaluation metrics.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds HyPE success rates of 0.55±0.09, 0.13±0.10 and 0.00±0.00 for Key Turn, Object Hold and Pen Twirl; retained methods' entries are unchanged. New Table 7 reports, for example, Hopper Hop correlations of 0.88 for IQ-MPC versus 0.49 for IQL+SAC. New findings also cover alpha sensitivity, noise degradation, computational cost and comparable performance with HyPE on Cheetah Run and Quadruped Run.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 adds a return-gap bound attributed to Kolev et al. Appendix G.3 introduces Gaussian and approximately matched-variance assumptions, then uses Pinsker's inequality and a KL derivation to connect consistency loss with transition-distribution error. V1's objective-equivalence and policy-update proofs are retained and renumbered.

C1.justification: The abstract and three contribution bullets retain the same central claims: reward-free world models for online imitation learning, planning without explicit reward modeling, strong complex-control performance and reward recovery. The shortened conclusion preserves this scope; the new analyses primarily support existing contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of regularization sensitivity and recovered-reward variance, acknowledges the method's primarily deterministic design, and discusses limited noise robustness and computational overhead. The introduction also shifts attribution for distribution-shift and bias mitigation from the novel formulation to online interaction. These substantially expand the interpretation and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: Appendix F newly specifies a single RTX 2080 Ti for the timing comparisons and reports training time in seconds. The detailed architecture and default hyperparameters in Appendix A remain unchanged, and no new code or data access information is provided.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to model-based imitation approaches including MAIL, EfficientImitate, V-MAIL, CMIL, Ditto and DMIL, alongside hybrid inverse RL and LS-IQ. The methodology now explicitly positions critic-derived rewards against prior approaches using separate reward models, sharpening a previously limited comparison with this literature.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify reward-free modeling and regularization, shorten the conclusion, and update affiliations and publication headers. Visual experiments and reward recovery move from the main text to Appendices E.4 and E.6. Much of the original prose and broad section sequence remains intact.

P2.justification: Figures 2–3 and Table 1 expand for HyPE, with revised legends and colors; Figures 12, 14 and 16 and Table 7 add new displays. Existing visual-control and reward-recovery plots are relocated. Figure 2 shortens Walker Run, Quadruped Run and Hopper Hop from 4M to 1M displayed steps, and Cheetah Run from 2M to 1M.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens comparative evaluation and support for reward recovery through HyPE comparisons, four-task correlation measurements, and sensitivity, noise and computational-cost analyses. These address important gaps in v1 and make performance limitations more assessable, including ties with HyPE and higher costs than model-free baselines. Four shorter learning-curve windows reduce long-horizon evidence, and the new theory remains assumption-dependent, but the additional comparative and diagnostic evidence provides a clear net improvement.
